When she feels threatened, a ball python rolls into a tight ball with her head tucked inside — that is where the name comes from.
Ball pythons come from the grasslands of West and Central Africa, spending hot days underground in burrows.
The pits along her lips sense infrared heat, so she can find a warm mouse in total darkness.
Ball pythons commonly live 20 to 30 years; one at the Saint Louis Zoo lived past 60.
Skipping meals for weeks — sometimes months — is normal for ball pythons, especially in the cooler season.
She is most active around dusk and at night; daytime is for hiding and digesting.
She sheds her skin in one piece, eyes included: cloudy blue eyes mean a shed is days away.
Moving between the hot side and the cool side is how she sets her own body temperature.
Her forked tongue carries scent to the Jacobson's organ in the roof of her mouth — that is how she smells.
Ancient Egyptians wore the rearing cobra, the uraeus, on the royal crown as a symbol of protection — a snake as royalty.
Her name is written in a cartouche: the oval ring Egyptians reserved for royal names.
Ball pythons are constrictors and not venomous; they are among the calmest snakes kept as pets.
Adult females are usually larger than males — three to five feet long and a few pounds.
Snakes never blink: a clear scale called the spectacle covers each eye and comes off with every shed.
A ball python's heart can shift position slightly to let large prey pass — everything about her is built for swallowing meals whole.
